prompt.context: Our client is a steel manufacturing company in the Netherlands. They are considering investing in an advanced analytics tool that will help them better predict inventory schedule. They are also looking at immediate methods to save costs.
prompt.question: A) Steel coils are currently transported from the factory to customers via Railways, Trucks, Vessels and Barges. Analyze these four transport methods and suggest any opportunities for cost saving. B) Suggest any alternative techniques to save cost in the immediate future.

clarifying_info.q: Does the company operate domestically or internationally?
clarifying_info.a: The company operates internationally in 100+ countries.
Customers are predominantly large B2B manufacturers with both short and long-term contracts.

clarifying_info.q: What products does the company make?
clarifying_info.a: For this case, assume steel is only manufactured as coils.

clarifying_info.q: Is there a specific cost-saving target?
clarifying_info.a: The objective is to identify cost savings with no particular target.

clarifying_info.q: What does utilization % mean in Exhibit 1?
clarifying_info.a: Utilization refers to the percentage of each vehicle's capacity that is used for steel coils. The remaining space is empty.

exhibits.title: Transport Methods Overview
exhibits.shows: A table comparing four transport modes (Rail, Truck, Barge, Vessel) across five metrics.

exhibits.title: Weekly Steel Coil Transfers from Pier to Trucks
exhibits.shows: A bar chart showing the number of steel coils transferred from the pier to trucks each week over 21 weeks, with a note that total volume for delivery is 5,700 steel coils and 1 steel coil equals 10 tons.

data.notable: Elevated coil transfers to trucks visible in weeks 1 and 2

framework: Cover the cost structure and drivers for each of the four transport modes (Rail, Truck, Barge, Vessel)
Evaluate current utilization rates vs. full capacity to identify efficiency gaps
Calculate total weekly cost and cost-saving potential per mode by closing the utilization gap
Address Part B: identify alternative/immediate cost-saving levers beyond transport capacity optimization
Incorporate steel-industry specifics: B2B contracts, international reach, coil-only format
Close with a prioritized recommendation and risks

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 1, calculate the weekly volume, weekly cost, and cost-saving potential for each transport mode.
questions.guidance: Candidate should multiply Deliveries/Week by Volume/Delivery to get weekly volume, then multiply by Cost/ton for weekly spend, then apply (100% - Utilization%) to get maximum savings from filling empty capacity.

math.setup: For each mode: Volume/week = Deliveries/Week x Volume/Delivery (ton). Cost/week = Volume/week x Cost ($/ton). Cost saving potential = Cost/week x (1 - Utilization%).

questions.prompt: Why is the usage of trucks so high, and what does Exhibit 2 reveal about the relationship between vessel and truck deliveries?
questions.guidance: Vessels are loaded every 14 days and run at 100% capacity, but trucks leave daily. The chart shows that in weeks 1 and 2 a large number of coils are transferred from the pier to trucks — suggesting that when a vessel offloads, some coils that cannot be stored are immediately re-routed to trucks. Weeks 3 onwards the bar chart returns to lower levels, implying better inventory management could eliminate most of the excess truck usage.

math.setup: Identify coils going to trucks in weeks 1-2 that could be avoided with better inventory management. Total coils in chart = 5,700. Coils unavoidable (weeks 1-2 combined) = 3,000. Avoidable coils = 5,700 - 3,000 = 2,700 coils. Each coil = 10 tons. Truck cost = $30/ton, Vessel cost = $10/ton, differential = $20/ton.
math.answer: $540,000 in savings by avoiding unnecessary pier-to-truck transfers

brainstorming.prompt: Beyond transport capacity optimization, what other immediate cost-saving techniques could the client pursue?

categories.name: Procurement & Supplier
ideas: Renegotiate cost/ton rates with carriers given volume leverage
Consolidate vendors to achieve volume discounts
Audit supplier contracts for hidden fees or unfavorable terms

categories.name: Operations & Inventory
ideas: Implement better demand forecasting to reduce safety stock and holding costs
Align delivery schedules to reduce idle vehicles and waiting time
Reduce vessel KPI from 100% to 95% utilization to prevent pier overflow and costly truck re-routing
Use the advanced analytics tool already under consideration to improve inventory scheduling

categories.name: Transport Mix Optimization
ideas: Shift volume from high-cost trucks ($30/ton) to lower-cost vessels ($10/ton) and rail ($25/ton) where geography allows
Reduce number of truck runs by batching deliveries to nearby customers
Evaluate whether barge frequency (every 20 days) can be increased to reduce dependence on trucks

categories.name: Workforce & Contracts
ideas: Review labor contracts for truck drivers (potential unionization risk)
Explore flexible staffing for peak loading periods
Incentivize carriers for fuller loads through performance-based pricing

categories.name: Technology & Analytics
ideas: Accelerate the advanced analytics tool investment to improve inventory prediction
Use real-time tracking to dynamically re-route shipments to cheapest available mode
Digitize order management to reduce scheduling errors that lead to rush truck deployments

recommendation: Drive total cost savings of approximately $7.84M: $7.3M from better capacity utilization across Rail, Truck, and Barge, and $540K from improved vessel inventory management to avoid pier-to-truck overflow
Continue to invest in the advanced analytics tool, which directly addresses the identified inventory management cost driver and will compound savings over time
risks: Utilization assumptions may not hold if demand patterns vary; average utilization used here may overstate saving potential
Truck drivers may be unionized; reducing truck runs could require contract renegotiation, slowing implementation
Vessels running at 95% instead of 100% may require changes to labor KPIs and could face operational resistance
Inventory improvements depend on customer cooperation around delivery scheduling
next_steps: Modify vessel labor KPIs from 100% to 95% utilization target to reduce pier overflow and reliance on expensive trucks
Gradually reduce the number of truck runs to improve utilization from 75% toward 100%
Renegotiate cost/ton rates with carriers where possible given volume scale
Accelerate the advanced analytics tool rollout to institutionalize inventory management improvements
